concepts.name: Nature, features, classification and criticism of the Fundamental Rights
concepts.description: Part III (Articles 12-35), its features, classification and criticism.
concepts.idea: The Fundamental Rights are justiciable, qualified guarantees, some for citizens only and some for all persons.
concepts.rule: Part III covers Articles 12 to 35 and is called the Magna Carta of India (p.127). Originally there were seven rights; the right to property was deleted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, leaving six (p.127). The rights are not absolute: the State may impose reasonable restrictions, and the courts decide their reasonableness (p.129). Parliament can curtail them only by a constitutional amendment, not an ordinary act, and not so as to affect the basic structure (p.129). Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended in a National Emergency, and Article 19 is suspended automatically only in an external emergency (p.131). Table 8.2 separates the rights of citizens only (Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30) from those also open to foreigners (p.130).
concepts.example: A foreigner can claim Article 21 but not Article 16.

questions.q: Part III of the Constitution is described as the 'Magna Carta' of India. The original Magna Carta, which Laxmikanth calls the first written document relating to the Fundamental Rights of citizens, was issued by
o: King Edward I of England in 1297
King Charles I of England in 1628
King William III of England in 1689
questions.e: p.127 and fn 1 (p.171): Part III is described as the Magna Carta of India; the Magna Carta is the Charter of Rights issued by King John of England in 1215 under pressure from the barons, the first written document relating to the Fundamental Rights of citizens.
w: King Edward I's 1297 act only confirmed the charter; the Charter was issued under pressure from the barons in 1215 (fn 1, p.171).
1628 is the Petition of Right, a different document; the Magna Carta was issued in 1215 (fn 1, p.171).
1689 is the English Bill of Rights, a different document; the Magna Carta dates from 1215 (fn 1, p.171).

questions.q: During a National Emergency, the six rights guaranteed by Article 19 are suspended automatically only when the emergency has been declared on the ground of
o: war, external aggression or armed rebellion alike
failure of the constitutional machinery in a state
questions.e: p.131: the six rights of Article 19 are automatically suspended only when emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression (external emergency) and not on the ground of armed rebellion (internal emergency).
w: Armed rebellion (internal emergency) does not automatically suspend Article 19 (p.131).
The automatic suspension is confined to the external ground; it does not extend to armed rebellion (p.131).
Failure of the constitutional machinery is a state-level President's rule ground, not a ground of National Emergency (p.131, p.163).

questions.q: The Constitution provides that the Fundamental Rights can be suspended during a National Emergency, except those guaranteed by
questions.e: p.131: the Fundamental Rights can be suspended during a National Emergency except the rights guaranteed by Articles 20 and 21.
w: Article 19 is suspended automatically in an external emergency (p.131).
Article 22 is not exempted; only Articles 20 and 21 stand outside the suspension (p.131).
Neither Article 14 nor Article 32 is an exempted right; the exception is Articles 20 and 21 (p.131).

questions.q: Who is credited in Laxmikanth with the remark that the Constitution of India is a 'paradise for lawyers'?
questions.e: p.167: critics allege the Constitution was made by lawyers for lawyers, and Sir Ivor Jennings called it a 'paradise for lawyers'.
w: Kapoor is cited for saying the chapter should be renamed 'Limitations on Fundamental Rights', not for this remark (p.166).
Dicey is cited for the Rule of Law, not for this remark (p.133).
Ambedkar is cited for calling Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution (p.158), not for this remark.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the features of the Fundamental Rights:

1. The Fundamental Rights are guaranteed to all persons and every one of them is available to citizens and foreigners alike.
2. Whether a restriction imposed by the State on a Fundamental Right is reasonable is to be decided by the courts.
3. Some of the Fundamental Rights are available even against the action of private individuals.
4. Parliament can curtail or repeal the Fundamental Rights by an ordinary act of Parliament.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: Some are available only to citizens, others to all persons (p.128, Table 8.2 p.130). Statement 2 is correct: p.129 says the courts decide whether the restrictions are reasonable. Statement 3 is correct: p.129: all are available against arbitrary State action, but some also against private individuals. Statement 4 is incorrect: p.129: only by a constitutional amendment act, not an ordinary act.
w: '1 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.128
'2 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.128
'2 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.128

concepts.name: Definition of State, laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights, and Article 14
concepts.description: Article 12 (State), Article 13 (laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights) and Article 14 with the Rule of Law and exceptions to equality.
concepts.idea: The State is defined widely, laws against the rights are void, and equality before law admits only reasonable classification.
concepts.rule: Article 12 includes the Union and state governments and legislatures, local authorities and other authorities such as LIC, ONGC and SAIL (p.131). Article 13 voids inconsistent laws and its 'law' covers ordinances, delegated legislation and custom with the force of law (p.132). A constitutional amendment is not 'law' under Article 13, but Kesavananda Bharati (1973) allows challenge on the basic structure (p.132). Article 14 applies to all persons and permits reasonable classification on an intelligible differentia (p.132). Dicey's Rule of Law applies in India in its first two elements (p.133). Exceptions include Article 361 immunities, Articles 105 and 194, and Article 31C (pp.133-134).
concepts.example: A rule made by a department can be struck down under Article 13.

questions.q: According to Article 12 as explained by Laxmikanth, the 'local authorities' that form part of the State include
questions.a: municipalities, panchayats, district boards and improvement trusts
o: municipalities, panchayats, district boards and improvement trusts
only the executive and legislative organs of the Union and the states
questions.e: p.131: the State includes (3) all local authorities, that is, municipalities, panchayats, district boards, improvement trusts etc., and (4) all other authorities, statutory or non-statutory, like LIC, ONGC, SAIL.
w: District boards and improvement trusts are also listed, so 'only' municipalities and panchayats is too narrow (p.131).
LIC, ONGC and SAIL are the examples given for 'all other authorities', not for local authorities (p.131).
The organs of the Union and state governments are separate heads of the definition, not local authorities (p.131).

questions.q: In Article 14, the concept of 'equality before law' is of ______ origin, while the concept of 'equal protection of laws' has been taken from the ______.
questions.e: p.132: 'equality before law' is of British origin while 'equal protection of laws' has been taken from the American Constitution.
w: The two origins are swapped in this option (p.132).
The second concept is American, not Irish (p.132).
The first concept is British, not French (p.132).

questions.q: Article 13 states that a constitutional amendment is not a 'law' for its purposes. In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court nevertheless held that a constitutional amendment can be declared void if it
questions.a: violates a fundamental right that forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution
o: violates a fundamental right that forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution
violates any Fundamental Right, whether or not it forms part of the basic structure
was passed while a National Emergency was in force
was not first referred to the Supreme Court for its opinion
questions.e: p.132: Article 13 declares an amendment is not a law, but Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that an amendment violating a fundamental right that forms part of the basic structure can be declared void.
w: The test is the basic structure; not every Fundamental Right is a part of it (p.132).
The chapter attaches no such condition to the timing of an amendment (p.132).
No prior reference to the Court is required; the challenge is on the ground of the basic structure (p.132).

questions.q: For a classification of persons to survive Article 14, the Supreme Court requires it to be based on
questions.a: an intelligible differential and substantial distinction, and not to be arbitrary, artificial or evasive
o: an intelligible differential and substantial distinction, and not to be arbitrary, artificial or evasive
equal treatment of every person, with no classification of any kind
the discretion of the administering authority, if a statute confers it
any distinction that the legislature chooses to make
questions.e: p.132: Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification; the classification should not be arbitrary, artificial or evasive but based on an intelligible differential and substantial distinction.
w: Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification (p.132).
The classification must not be arbitrary, so unfettered discretion does not suffice (p.132).
The legislature's choice alone is not enough; the distinction must be intelligible and substantial (p.132).

questions.q: Under Article 361, civil proceedings in respect of an act done in his or her personal capacity may be instituted against the President or a Governor during the term of office only after
questions.a: two months have expired after notice has been delivered to him or her
o: two months have expired after notice has been delivered to him or her
one month has expired after notice has been delivered to him or her
six months have expired after notice has been delivered to him or her
the President or Governor has ceased to hold office
questions.e: p.133: no civil proceedings in respect of an act done in a personal capacity shall be instituted during the term until the expiration of two months next after notice has been delivered.
w: The period is two months, not one (p.133).
The period is two months, not six (p.133).
Civil proceedings for personal acts are allowed during the term after notice; it is criminal proceedings that cannot be instituted or continued (p.133).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the exceptions to equality before the law, as described by Laxmikanth:

1. Criminal proceedings may be instituted against the President during the term of office but may not be continued.
2. No member of Parliament is liable to any court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in Parliament or any committee of it.
3. Article 105 gives the same protection to the members of a state legislature.
4. Article 361-A protects a substantially true report of the proceedings of a House only if it is published in a newspaper and not if broadcast on radio or television.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: p.133: no criminal proceedings shall be instituted or continued during the term of office (Article 361). Statement 2 is correct: p.133: Article 105. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.133: that protection comes from Article 194. Statement 4 is incorrect: p.133: publication in a newspaper or by radio or television is covered.
w: '1 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.133

2. Foreign sovereigns, ambassadors and diplomats enjoy immunity from criminal and civil proceedings.
3. No member of Parliament is liable to court proceedings for a vote given in a committee of the House (Article 105).
4. The UNO and its agencies enjoy diplomatic immunity.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.133. Statement 2 is correct: p.134. Statement 3 is correct: p.133. Statement 4 is correct: p.134. So exactly 4 are correct.

concepts.name: Articles 15 and 16: non-discrimination, equality of opportunity and reservation
concepts.description: Articles 15 and 16, reservation, the creamy layer, EWS quota, Mandal Commission and Indra Sawhney.
concepts.idea: Articles 15 and 16 bar discrimination but allow special provision for women, backward classes and economically weaker sections.
concepts.rule: Article 15(1) bars discrimination by the State on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, while 15(2) also binds private persons (p.134). Clauses 15(4), 15(5) and 15(6) came by the 1st (1951), 93rd (2005) and 103rd (2019) Amendments (p.135). Article 16 adds descent and residence as grounds and allows reservation under 16(4), 16(4A), 16(4B) and 16(6) (pp.137-138). Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld 27% OBC reservation with the creamy layer excluded, a 50% limit and no reservation in promotions (p.139). The 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments responded to parts of that ruling (p.140). The creamy-layer ceiling rose from Rs 1 lakh (1993) to Rs 8 lakh (2017) (p.136).
concepts.example: A state may reserve promotion posts for SCs and STs under Article 16(4A).

questions.q: Article 15(5), which lets the State make special provision for backward classes and the SCs and STs in admission to educational institutions, including private institutions aided or unaided by the State (except minority institutions), was added by
questions.e: p.134-135 and Table 8.3: Article 15(5) was added by the 93rd Amendment Act, 2005; Article 15(4) by the 1st Amendment, 1951; Article 15(6) by the 103rd Amendment, 2019.
w: The 1st Amendment added Article 15(4), the general special provision for backward classes (p.135).
The 103rd Amendment added Article 15(6) for economically weaker sections (p.135).
The 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A, not a clause of Article 15 (p.150).

Indira Gandhi's government is not credited with appointing it; the text names the Morarji Desai Government (p.139).
The Narasimha Rao Government introduced two changes in 1991, after the report (p.139).

Consider the following statements about Article 15:

concepts.name: Articles 17, 18, 23 and 24: untouchability, titles, forced labour and child labour
concepts.description: Articles 17, 18, 23 and 24: untouchability, titles, forced labour and child labour.
concepts.idea: These Articles abolish social evils and bind private persons in some cases.
concepts.rule: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its enforcement an offence; the 1955 Act was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976 (pp.140-141). The Supreme Court held in the PUDR case (1982) that Article 17 operates against private individuals (p.141). Article 18 bars titles except military and academic ones; Balaji Raghavan (1995) held National Awards are not titles (p.141). Article 23 bans traffic in human beings and forced labour against the State and private persons (p.153). Article 24 bars employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work (p.154). The Child Labour Act, 1986 was renamed in 2016 (p.154).
concepts.example: A Padma award may not be used as a prefix to a name.

questions.q: The Supreme Court held that the right under Article 17 is available against private individuals, and that it is the constitutional obligation of the State to ensure that the right is not violated, in the
questions.a: People's Union for Democratic Rights case (1982)
o: People's Union for Democratic Rights case (1982)
Balaji Raghavan vs. Union of India (1995)
Indra Sawhney vs. Union of India (1992)
Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India (1978)
questions.e: p.141: in the People's Union for Democratic Rights case (1982) the Supreme Court held that Article 17 is available against private individuals and the State must act to ensure it is not violated.
w: Balaji Raghavan concerned national awards and Article 18 (p.141).
Indra Sawhney concerned reservation under Article 16(4) (p.139).
Maneka Gandhi concerned the wider reading of Article 21 (p.148).

concepts.name: Article 19: the six freedoms and the grounds of restriction
concepts.description: Article 19: the six freedoms and the grounds of restriction.
concepts.idea: Each Article 19 freedom is available to citizens and restricted only on the grounds stated in the Article.
concepts.rule: Article 19 guarantees six freedoms to citizens, protected only against State action (p.142). The right to property in 19(1)(f) was deleted in 1978 and co-operative societies were added in 2011 (pp.142, 172). Grounds of restriction on speech include sovereignty and integrity (16th Amendment, 1963) and public order (1st Amendment, 1951) (pp.142-143). Assembly must be peaceful, unarmed and on public land and does not include a right to strike (p.145). Association includes the negative right but not the right to recognition (p.145). In Anuradha Bhasin (2020) internet-based trade was protected under 19(1)(g), subject to proportionality (p.147).
concepts.example: A union can be formed freely but may not claim a right to strike.

concepts.name: Articles 20 and 22: conviction, arrest and preventive detention
concepts.description: Article 20 (conviction) and Article 22 (arrest and preventive detention).
concepts.idea: Article 20 limits punishment and Article 22 gives procedural safeguards on arrest and detention.
concepts.rule: Article 20 bars ex-post-facto criminal laws, double jeopardy and self-incrimination (p.147). The ex-post-facto bar does not cover civil or tax laws, and self-incrimination excludes blood specimens and signatures (p.147). Article 22 gives a person arrested under ordinary law the right to grounds, a lawyer and production before a magistrate within 24 hours (p.152). Preventive detention beyond three months needs an advisory board of high court judges; the 44th Amendment's two months is not in force (p.152). Parliament alone legislates on defence, foreign affairs and the security of India, while other grounds are concurrent (p.152). Laws such as PDA 1950, MISA, TADA and POTA were expired or repealed (p.153).
concepts.example: A detenu may be denied facts held against the public interest.

concepts.name: Articles 21 and 21A: life, personal liberty and the right to education
concepts.description: Article 21 (life and personal liberty) and Article 21A (elementary education).
concepts.idea: Article 21 was widened from procedure established by law to a fair, just and reasonable procedure.
concepts.rule: Article 21 is available to citizens and non-citizens (p.147). Gopalan (1950) read it narrowly against executive action only, and Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled it, introducing in effect due process (p.148). The Court has listed many rights under Article 21, such as privacy, shelter, livelihood and passive euthanasia (pp.148-149). Table 8.6 links cases such as Olga Tellis (livelihood) and Puttaswamy (privacy) with those rights (pp.150-151). Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment (2002), gives free and compulsory education to children aged six to fourteen (p.150). The RTE Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010 (p.151).
concepts.example: Hoskot (1978) is cited for the right to free legal aid.

concepts.name: Articles 25 to 30: freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights
concepts.description: Articles 25 to 30: freedom of religion and cultural and educational rights.
concepts.idea: Articles 25-28 protect religion and Articles 29-30 protect the culture and institutions of minorities.
concepts.rule: Article 25 protects individuals and Article 26 religious denominations, which must meet three conditions (pp.154-155). The right to propagate does not include conversion (p.154). Article 27 bars taxes, not fees, for promoting a religion (p.156). Article 28 prohibits religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions and makes it voluntary in recognised and aided ones (p.156). Article 29 protects any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture (p.156). Article 30 protects minorities' educational institutions, and the term minority is undefined (p.157).
concepts.example: A denomination can run its own charitable institutions under Article 26.

questions.q: Under Article 25, the right to propagate religion means
questions.a: the transmission of one's beliefs to others, without any right to convert another person
o: the transmission of one's beliefs to others, without any right to convert another person
the right to convert another person to one's own religion by any means short of force
the right to expound the tenets of one's religion only within one's own religious community
the right to receive State funds for spreading one's religion among others
questions.e: p.154: the right to propagate is the transmission and dissemination of one's religious beliefs to others or exposition of its tenets, but does not include a right to convert another person; forcible conversions impinge on the freedom of conscience.
w: Conversion of another person is expressly outside the right (p.154).
The text covers transmission of beliefs to others, not only within one's community (p.154).
Nothing in the chapter links the right to State funds; Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a religion (p.155).

questions.q: The rights of a religious denomination under Article 26 are subject to
questions.a: public order, morality and health, but not other Fundamental Rights provisions
o: public order, morality and health, but not other Fundamental Rights provisions
public order, morality, health and the other provisions relating to the Fundamental Rights
public order alone, with no other ground of restriction
the consent of the State government in every case of regulation
questions.e: p.155: like Article 25, Article 26 rights are subject to public order, morality and health, but unlike Article 25 they are not subject to other provisions relating to the Fundamental Rights.
w: That is the position of the individual's rights under Article 25, not Article 26 (p.155).
Morality and health are also grounds (p.155).
The chapter prescribes no requirement of State consent (p.155).

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT among the three conditions laid down by the Supreme Court for a religious denomination under Article 26?
questions.a: It should have a sacred scripture of its own
o: It should have a sacred scripture of its own
It should be a collection of individuals with a system of beliefs conducive to their spiritual well-being
It should have a common organisation
It should be designated by a distinctive name
questions.e: p.155: a denomination must be a collection of individuals with a system of beliefs regarded as conducive to spiritual well-being, have a common organisation and a distinctive name.
w: This is the first condition (p.155).
This is the second condition (p.155).
This is the third condition (p.155).

questions.q: Article 27 prohibits the levy of a tax for the promotion of any particular religion. What may the State legitimately levy on pilgrims or on religious endowments?
questions.a: A fee, for special services, safety measures or regulation expenditure
o: A fee, for special services, safety measures or regulation expenditure
A tax, to promote the religion of the majority of the people
A tax, to maintain a particular religious denomination
No levy of any kind, whether a tax or a fee
questions.e: p.156: Article 27 prohibits only a tax and not a fee, since a fee controls the secular administration of religious institutions; a fee can be levied on pilgrims for special service or safety, and on endowments for regulation expenditure.
w: Taxes for promotion of any particular religion are barred (p.155).
Taxes for the maintenance of a particular denomination are barred (p.155).
Article 27 prohibits only a tax and not a fee (p.156).

questions.q: Under Article 28, religious instruction is completely prohibited in
questions.a: educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
o: educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
institutions administered by the State but established under an endowment or trust
institutions receiving aid out of State funds
questions.e: p.156: religious instruction is completely prohibited in institutions wholly maintained by the State; permitted in State-administered endowment institutions; voluntary in recognised and aided institutions.
w: There it is permitted if the endowment or trust requires it (p.156).
In recognised institutions it is permitted on a voluntary basis (p.156).
In aided institutions it is permitted on a voluntary basis (p.156).

concepts.name: Article 32 and the writs
concepts.description: Article 32 and the five writs, with the contrast between Articles 32 and 226.
concepts.idea: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and the Supreme Court may not refuse it.
concepts.rule: Article 32 is a basic feature, called by Ambedkar the heart and soul of the Constitution (p.158). It can be suspended only as the Constitution provides, as under Article 359 (p.159). Its jurisdiction is original but not exclusive and is concurrent with Article 226 (p.159). The Supreme Court issues writs only for Fundamental Rights, while a high court may also do so for other purposes (p.160). Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo-warranto each have limits stated in the chapter (pp.160-161). Quo-warranto can be sought by any public-minded person (p.161).
concepts.example: A prisoner held without lawful authority can seek habeas corpus.

questions.q: The Supreme Court has ruled that Article 32 (the right to constitutional remedies) is
questions.a: a basic feature, which cannot be abridged even by an amendment
o: a basic feature, which cannot be abridged even by an amendment
a right which Parliament may abridge by an ordinary law of its own
a right which may be taken away by a constitutional amendment but not by an ordinary law
a right available only to citizens and not to other persons
questions.e: p.158: the Supreme Court has ruled that Article 32 is a basic feature of the Constitution and cannot be abridged or taken away even by way of an amendment.
w: Being a basic feature, it cannot be abridged even by an amendment, let alone an ordinary law (p.158).

questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.158. Statement 2 is correct: p.158. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.159: 'any other court' does not include the high courts, since Article 226 has already conferred these powers. Statement 4 is correct: p.159.

concepts.name: Articles 33 to 35, martial law, right to property and Articles 31A, 31B, 31C
concepts.description: Articles 33 to 35, martial law, the right to property and Articles 31A, 31B and 31C.
concepts.idea: Parliament may restrict rights for the forces, and certain laws are shielded from the rights.
concepts.rule: Article 33 lets Parliament alone restrict the rights of the armed forces, police and similar forces (p.161). Article 34 deals with martial law, which is implicit in the Constitution and differs from a National Emergency (pp.162-163). Article 35 vests power in Parliament alone to legislate for certain rights (p.163). The right to property was repealed in 1978 and survives as Article 300A (p.164). Article 31A saves five categories of laws from Articles 14 and 19, and Article 31B shields the Ninth Schedule (p.165). Coelho (2007) denied blanket immunity to the Ninth Schedule, and Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the extension of Article 31C (p.166).
concepts.example: A law in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 can be tested on the basic structure.

questions.q: The power under Article 33 to restrict or abrogate the Fundamental Rights of the members of the armed forces, para-military forces and police forces is conferred on
questions.a: Parliament alone, not the state legislatures
o: Parliament alone, not the state legislatures
Parliament and the state legislatures concurrently
the President, by an ordinance alone
questions.e: p.161: the power to make laws under Article 33 is conferred only on Parliament and not on the state legislatures.
w: The power is not shared with state legislatures (p.161).
The text vests the power in Parliament, by law (p.161).
The Court does not make this law; a law of Parliament under Article 33 cannot even be challenged in a court on Fundamental Rights grounds (p.161).

questions.q: Martial law differs from a National Emergency in that martial law
questions.a: suspends the government and the ordinary law courts
o: suspends the government and the ordinary law courts
continues the government and the ordinary law courts
can be imposed only on the grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion
has a specific and detailed provision in the Constitution
questions.e: Table 8.7, pp.162-163: martial law suspends the government and ordinary courts, is imposed for a breakdown of law and order due to any reason, in a specific area, and is implicit; a National Emergency is the reverse on each point.
w: That describes a National Emergency (Table 8.7, p.162).
Those three grounds belong to a National Emergency; martial law is imposed to restore a breakdown of law and order due to any reason (Table 8.7, p.163).
That is true of a National Emergency; martial law has no specific provision and is implicit (Table 8.7, p.163).

questions.q: Since the right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right, a person aggrieved by its violation can
questions.a: move the high court under Article 226, but not the Supreme Court under Article 32
o: move the high court under Article 226, but not the Supreme Court under Article 32
move the Supreme Court directly under Article 32 as a matter of right
move only the Supreme Court and not the high court at all
move no court whatever, as the right has been abolished
questions.e: p.164: in case of violation the aggrieved person cannot directly move the Supreme Court under Article 32 but can move the High Court under Article 226.
w: Article 32 is available only for Fundamental Rights (p.164).
The high court under Article 226 is open to the aggrieved person (p.164).
It remains a legal right under Article 300-A, though not a Fundamental Right (p.164).

questions.q: In the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the Supreme Court ruled that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge if they violate
questions.a: Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 or the basic structure
o: Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 or the basic structure
only the basic structure, and not any Fundamental Right as such
no ground, since the Ninth Schedule gives blanket immunity
questions.e: p.166: I.R. Coelho held there can be no blanket immunity; laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be challenged if they violate Articles 14, 15, 19 or 21 or the basic structure.
w: Those two Articles are the ones mentioned for Articles 31A and 31C, not the full list in Coelho (p.166).
Coelho named Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 as well as the basic structure (p.166).
The Court ruled that there could not be any blanket immunity (p.166).

questions.q: In the Minerva Mills case (1980), the Supreme Court declared unconstitutional and invalid
questions.a: the 42nd Amendment's extension of the protection of Article 31C to all the Directive Principles
o: the 42nd Amendment's extension of the protection of Article 31C to all the Directive Principles
the protection of laws implementing Article 39(b) or (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19
the 44th Amendment's deletion of the right to property
the inclusion of the original acts in the Ninth Schedule
questions.e: p.166: the 42nd Amendment extended Article 31C to any directive principle of Part IV, and the Supreme Court declared this extension unconstitutional in Minerva Mills (1980).
w: That protection was held constitutional and valid in Kesavananda Bharati (p.166).
The deletion of the right to property was not struck down; it stands (p.164).
The chapter does not link Minerva Mills with the Ninth Schedule (p.166).

2. At present the actual total number of acts and regulations in it is 282.
3. The acts and regulations of the state legislatures in it deal with land reforms and the abolition of the zamindari system.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.166. Statement 2 is correct: fn 20, p.172: the last entry is numbered 284 but three entries were deleted and one numbered 257A. Statement 3 is correct: p.166. So exactly 3 are correct.
w: 'None' miscounts: exactly 3 are correct (statements 1, 2, 3).
'Only one' miscounts: exactly 3 are correct (statements 1, 2, 3).
'Only two' miscounts: exactly 3 are correct (statements 1, 2, 3).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Ninth Schedule and judicial review:

1. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held the acts in the Ninth Schedule open to challenge as violating the basic structure.
2. In Waman Rao (1980), the Court held that acts included after 24 April 1973 are valid only if they do not damage the basic structure.
3. In I.R. Coelho (2007), the Court held that judicial review is a basic feature that cannot be taken away by putting a law in the Ninth Schedule.
4. Article 31B, along with the Ninth Schedule, was added by the 1st Amendment Act, 1951.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.165. Statement 2 is correct: p.165. Statement 3 is correct: p.166. Statement 4 is correct: fn 18, p.172. So exactly 4 are correct.
w: 'Only one' miscounts: exactly 4 are correct (statements 1, 2, 3, 4).
'Only two' miscounts: exactly 4 are correct (statements 1, 2, 3, 4).
'Only three' miscounts: exactly 4 are correct (statements 1, 2, 3, 4).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 31C:

1. In Kesavananda Bharati, the Supreme Court held valid the provision barring courts from questioning a law that carries a declaration of giving effect to the policy.
2. In Kesavananda Bharati, the Court declared the protection of laws implementing Article 39(b) or (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 unconstitutional.
3. The 42nd Amendment extended the protection of Article 31C to the Fundamental Duties.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: p.166: that provision was declared unconstitutional and invalid. Statement 2 is incorrect: p.166: that provision was held constitutional and valid. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.166: to the directive principles of Part IV. So none is correct.
w: 'Only one' miscounts: none is correct.
'Only two' miscounts: none is correct.
'All three' miscounts: none is correct.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: p.164. Statement-II is correct: pp.163-164. The two statements are separate features of Article 35; the obligation to legislate does not account for the extension of competence (pp.163-164).
w: Rejected: Statement-II does not explain Statement-I: The two statements are separate features of Article 35; the obligation to legislate does not account for the extension of competence (pp.163-164).
